answers: Run the instance in an Auto Scaling group with min/max/desired capacity of 1 spanning multiple AZs
Front the instance with a load balancer health check so failures are detected at the application level
explanation: A "min 1, max 1" ASG is the self-healing pattern for stateful singletons: when the instance or its AZ dies, the ASG launches a replacement in a surviving AZ. The load balancer adds application-level health detection (and a stable endpoint while the instance is replaced). The exam guide calls this out as improving reliability "when application changes are not possible" — refactoring violates the constraint, and reboots/resizing don't address failures.

question: A developer accidentally ran a destructive UPDATE against production RDS at 14:32. The database has automated backups with 7-day retention. What is the best recovery option?
options: Point-in-time restore to a new instance at 14:31 and recover the affected data
Reboot the instance to roll back uncommitted transactions
Restore last night's manual snapshot over the current instance
Enable Multi-AZ and fail over to the standby
answer: Point-in-time restore to a new instance at 14:31 and recover the affected data
explanation: Automated backups combine daily snapshots with continuous transaction logs, allowing restore to any second within retention (up to the last ~5 minutes). PITR creates a *new* instance at the chosen moment — you then copy the affected rows back, losing only what changed in one minute. A reboot can't undo committed writes; last night's snapshot discards a full day; the Multi-AZ standby faithfully replicated the bad UPDATE too — replication is not a backup.

question: An Auto Scaling group has 8 instances in AZ-a and 2 in AZ-b behind a load balancer. Users report inconsistent performance — instances in AZ-b receive far more traffic per instance. What balances the per-instance load?
options: Enable cross-zone load balancing so traffic distributes evenly across all instances regardless of AZ
Add more instances to AZ-b manually
Switch the ALB to least-connections routing
Create a separate load balancer per AZ
answer: Enable cross-zone load balancing so traffic distributes evenly across all instances regardless of AZ
explanation: Without cross-zone load balancing, each load balancer node splits traffic 50/50 between AZs — so AZ-b's 2 instances share the same half that AZ-a's 8 share, getting 4× the per-instance load. Cross-zone distributes across all 10 instances equally. It's on by default for ALB but *off* by default for NLB — a favorite exam detail. The other options treat symptoms or add complexity.

question: When orders change status, several systems (email, analytics, inventory, plus future additions) must react — each filtering for only the event types it cares about. The order service should not know its consumers. Which service fits best?
options: Amazon EventBridge with rules routing filtered events to each target
Direct SDK calls from the order service to each downstream system
A shared database table that consumers poll for changes
An SQS queue that all systems read from
answer: Amazon EventBridge with rules routing filtered events to each target
explanation: EventBridge is the event bus for exactly this: producers publish once, rules pattern-match event content and route to many targets (Lambda, SQS, Step Functions, APIs), and new consumers mean a new rule — the producer never changes. Direct calls couple the producer to every consumer; polling a table adds latency and load; one shared SQS queue delivers each message to a single consumer, not to all of them.

question: A company must apply one consistent backup policy — daily backups, 35-day retention, copies to a second Region — across its EBS volumes, RDS databases, DynamoDB tables, and EFS file systems, with compliance reporting. Which service does this centrally?
options: AWS Backup with a backup plan assigned to tagged resources
Separate snapshot scripts per service triggered by cron
S3 lifecycle rules
AWS Config
answer: AWS Backup with a backup plan assigned to tagged resources
explanation: AWS Backup is the single control plane for backups across a dozen-plus services: plans define schedule/retention/cross-Region copy, resources join by tag or ARN, vaults can be locked (WORM), and audit reporting is built in. Per-service scripts are exactly the sprawl it replaces; S3 lifecycle manages storage classes of existing objects; Config records configuration, not data.

question: A marketing site is fully static (HTML, CSS, JS, images). It currently runs on one EC2 instance, which has failed twice during campaigns. Which combination gives the site the highest availability with the LEAST operational effort? (Select TWO)
options: Host the static files in Amazon S3 with static website hosting
Serve the site through an Amazon CloudFront distribution
Move the site to a larger EC2 instance with daily AMI backups
Run nginx on two EC2 instances behind an ALB
Store the files on an EFS volume mounted to the existing instance
answers: Host the static files in Amazon S3 with static website hosting
Serve the site through an Amazon CloudFront distribution
explanation: Static content needs no servers at all: S3 provides 11-nines durable, regionally redundant hosting, and CloudFront adds global caching, HTTPS, and absorbs traffic spikes. Nothing to patch, no instances to fail — strictly more available than any EC2 arrangement and cheaper too. The EC2/EFS options keep operating servers to serve files that don't need one.

question: A trading platform sees a massive, predictable traffic spike every weekday at exactly 9:00 AM when markets open. Dynamic scaling reacts too slowly, causing 10 minutes of degraded service. What should the architect add?
options: A scheduled scaling action that increases desired capacity shortly before 9:00 AM on weekdays
A higher CPU threshold on the existing target tracking policy
Smaller instances so they launch faster
A second metric alarm on memory usage
answer: A scheduled scaling action that increases desired capacity shortly before 9:00 AM on weekdays
explanation: Reactive policies by definition scale *after* load arrives — boot plus warm-up time creates the 10-minute gap. For a known schedule, scheduled actions pre-provision capacity (e.g. at 8:45) so instances are in service when the spike hits; predictive scaling is the ML alternative when the pattern is regular but not clock-exact. Threshold and metric tweaks still react after the fact.

question: An application calling AWS APIs occasionally receives ThrottlingException errors during bursts. Retrying immediately makes the problem worse. What is the AWS-recommended client-side pattern?
options: Retries with exponential backoff and jitter
Retrying in a tight loop until the call succeeds
Catching and ignoring the throttling errors
Switching all API calls to a single sequential worker permanently
answer: Retries with exponential backoff and jitter
explanation: Exponential backoff spreads retries out (1s, 2s, 4s…) so a throttled fleet doesn't immediately re-stampede the API, and jitter (randomization) prevents synchronized retry waves from clients that were throttled together. AWS SDKs implement this by default. Tight loops amplify throttling; ignoring errors drops work; permanent serialization sacrifices throughput to avoid a transient condition.

question: A critical public API must keep working even if its entire primary AWS Region fails. Which combination of actions provides Regional failover? (Select TWO)
options: Deploy a full copy of the API stack in a second Region
Use Route 53 failover routing with health checks to switch DNS to the second Region when the primary fails
Add more Availability Zones to the existing Region's deployment
Enable cross-zone load balancing on the existing ALB
Increase the existing Auto Scaling group's maximum capacity
answers: Deploy a full copy of the API stack in a second Region
Use Route 53 failover routing with health checks to switch DNS to the second Region when the primary fails
explanation: Region-level resilience needs two things: a stack that exists somewhere else (warm standby or active-active in Region 2, with data replicated), and a traffic-steering mechanism that notices the failure and redirects — Route 53 failover records with health checks (or Global Accelerator endpoint failover). More AZs, cross-zone balancing, and bigger ASGs all harden *within* the Region that just failed.

question: An application is deployed in three Regions. Every user should be routed to the Region that gives THEM the fastest response, and unhealthy Regions must be taken out of rotation automatically. Which Route 53 configuration fits?
options: Latency-based routing records with health checks on each Regional endpoint
Geolocation routing mapping each continent to a fixed Region
A failover policy with one primary and two secondaries
Simple records returning all three Regional IPs
answer: Latency-based routing records with health checks on each Regional endpoint
explanation: Latency-based routing answers each DNS query with the Region that has the lowest measured network latency for that user — not necessarily the geographically nearest — and health checks remove failing Regions from consideration. Geolocation is for compliance/content localization (fixed mapping, even when slow); failover is active-passive, wasting two Regions; simple records do no steering and no health awareness.

question: A gaming company needs an in-memory store for real-time leaderboards (sorted rankings), with replication and automatic failover for high availability, plus persistence options. Which engine should they choose?
options: ElastiCache for Redis
ElastiCache for Memcached
DynamoDB standard tables
RDS MySQL with a large buffer pool
answer: ElastiCache for Redis
explanation: The requirements map to Redis features: sorted sets are purpose-built for leaderboards, and Redis supports replication, Multi-AZ automatic failover, snapshots/AOF persistence, and pub/sub. Memcached is the simpler engine — multithreaded and easy to scale out, but no replication, persistence, or rich data structures. The Redis-vs-Memcached feature split is a reliable exam question.

question: A DynamoDB table uses `status` (values: ACTIVE, INACTIVE) as its partition key. The table is heavily throttled even though provisioned capacity far exceeds total traffic. What is the root cause?
options: The low-cardinality partition key concentrates traffic on one or two partitions (hot partitions), exceeding per-partition limits
DynamoDB tables require a sort key to scale
The table needs a global secondary index to spread load
Provisioned capacity applies per item, not per table
answer: The low-cardinality partition key concentrates traffic on one or two partitions (hot partitions), exceeding per-partition limits
explanation: DynamoDB spreads data and throughput across partitions by hashing the partition key. With only two possible values, virtually all traffic lands on two partitions — each capped at 3,000 RCU / 1,000 WCU — so the table throttles while aggregate capacity sits idle. The fix is a high-cardinality key (user ID, order ID), possibly with write sharding. Sort keys and GSIs don't repair a degenerate partition key choice.

question: Consumers poll an SQS queue continuously. Most ReceiveMessage calls return empty, driving up API costs and CPU. What is the recommended fix?
options: Enable long polling by setting ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds up to 20 seconds
Poll less frequently with a 5-minute sleep between calls
Switch to a FIFO queue
Increase the visibility timeout
answer: Enable long polling by setting ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds up to 20 seconds
explanation: Long polling holds the ReceiveMessage call open (up to 20 s) until a message arrives or the wait expires — eliminating the empty-response storm, cutting API calls (cost) dramatically, and *reducing* delivery latency versus sleeping between polls. Five-minute sleeps add up to 5 minutes of latency; FIFO changes ordering semantics; visibility timeout governs in-flight message invisibility, not polling behavior.

question: A customer-facing API built on Lambda shows occasional latency spikes of 1–2 seconds on the first request after idle periods, while typical requests take 50 ms. Which feature removes these spikes?
options: Provisioned concurrency on the function's production alias
A larger memory allocation
Reserved concurrency
Moving the function code to a container image
answer: Provisioned concurrency on the function's production alias
explanation: The spikes are cold starts — initializing a new execution environment. Provisioned concurrency keeps a configured number of environments initialized and warm, so requests hit pre-warmed instances at steady latency. More memory speeds execution but doesn't prevent initialization; *reserved* concurrency is a limit/guarantee on concurrent executions (a different knob with a confusingly similar name — classic exam distractor); container images generally cold-start slower, not faster.

question: A machine-learning team runs distributed training on hundreds of EC2 instances that need a shared POSIX file system with sub-millisecond latency and hundreds of GB/s of aggregate throughput, sourcing training data from S3. Which storage service fits?
options: Amazon FSx for Lustre with an S3-linked data repository
Amazon EFS Standard
Amazon S3 mounted via Mountpoint on each node
A large gp3 EBS volume attached to the head node and shared over NFS
answer: Amazon FSx for Lustre with an S3-linked data repository
explanation: FSx for Lustre is the HPC/ML file system: parallel architecture delivering hundreds of GB/s and sub-millisecond latencies, with data repository association that lazy-loads from and writes back to S3. EFS is general-purpose NFS — solid, but not in Lustre's performance class for this pattern. Mountpoint for S3 suits sequential object access, not POSIX random I/O; one instance re-exporting an EBS volume bottlenecks the entire cluster.

question: A company is moving a Windows application that requires shared SMB file storage with Active Directory integration and NTFS permissions. Which AWS service provides this?
options: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon EFS
Amazon S3
Amazon FSx for Lustre
answer: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
explanation: FSx for Windows is a fully managed native Windows file system: SMB protocol, NTFS, DFS namespaces, and AD integration (AWS managed AD or self-managed). EFS speaks NFS — Linux territory; S3 is object storage, not a file share; FSx for Lustre targets Linux HPC. The protocol is the tell: SMB/AD → FSx for Windows, NFS/Linux → EFS, parallel HPC → Lustre.

question: Application logs must be streamed into S3 (and optionally Redshift) in near real time, with optional transformation via Lambda — and the team wants zero servers, shards, or consumer applications to manage. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with a custom consumer
Amazon SQS with a fleet of worker instances
AWS DataSync on a schedule
answer: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
explanation: Firehose is the fully managed delivery pipe: it batches, optionally transforms (Lambda) and converts formats, and delivers to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, and third parties — no shards to size, no consumers to write, scaling handled. Kinesis Data Streams is the answer when you need custom real-time consumers or replay; SQS+workers is hand-built plumbing; DataSync moves file systems, not streams. "Easiest way to load streaming data into X" → Firehose.

question: Analysts run complex aggregation queries joining billions of rows of sales history for BI dashboards. The current RDS PostgreSQL instance takes minutes per query. Which service is purpose-built for this workload?
options: Amazon Redshift
A larger RDS PostgreSQL instance
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon ElastiCache
answer: Amazon Redshift
explanation: This is OLAP — scanning and aggregating huge datasets — and Redshift's columnar storage, compression, and massively parallel processing are built for it, routinely turning minutes into seconds at petabyte scale. RDS is row-oriented OLTP; scaling it up delays the wall. DynamoDB serves key-based access patterns, not ad-hoc joins; ElastiCache accelerates repeated reads, not novel analytical queries. OLTP→RDS, OLAP→Redshift is core exam vocabulary.

question: An e-commerce site needs product search with full-text queries, fuzzy matching for typos, filters, and relevance ranking. Which AWS service is designed for this?
options: Amazon OpenSearch Service
Amazon RDS with LIKE queries
Amazon DynamoDB with scan operations
Amazon Athena
answer: Amazon OpenSearch Service
explanation: OpenSearch (the Elasticsearch fork) is the managed search engine: inverted indexes for full-text search, fuzzy matching, faceted filtering, and relevance scoring out of the box. SQL `LIKE '%term%'` can't use indexes and offers no ranking; DynamoDB scans are expensive table reads with no text awareness; Athena is batch SQL over S3, not an interactive search backend.

question: A tightly coupled simulation across a fleet of EC2 instances is bottlenecked by inter-node network latency and throughput. Which combination of changes improves node-to-node network performance? (Select TWO)
options: Use instance types with enhanced networking (ENA) and high network bandwidth
Launch the fleet in a cluster placement group in one AZ
Spread the instances across three Regions for more total bandwidth
Attach larger EBS volumes to every node
Put an Application Load Balancer between the nodes
answers: Use instance types with enhanced networking (ENA) and high network bandwidth
Launch the fleet in a cluster placement group in one AZ
explanation: Two complementary levers: enhanced networking (ENA, and EFA for MPI-style HPC) raises per-instance packet rates and lowers latency, while a cluster placement group physically co-locates the fleet on a low-latency, high-bisection network segment. Spreading across Regions multiplies latency by orders of magnitude; EBS is storage, not network; an ALB is an HTTP front door, not an inter-node fabric.

question: An Aurora cluster has one writer and four read replicas. The application should spread its read queries across all replicas automatically, including ones added later by replica auto scaling. What should the application connect to?
options: The cluster's reader endpoint
The cluster endpoint
Each replica's instance endpoint, in rotation managed by application code
The writer's IP address
answer: The cluster's reader endpoint
explanation: Aurora's reader endpoint load-balances connections across all current read replicas — replicas added or removed by auto scaling join and leave automatically, no application changes. The cluster endpoint always targets the writer (use it for writes); hand-rolled rotation over instance endpoints breaks every time the replica set changes; raw IPs break on failover.

question: A REST API on API Gateway serves catalog data that changes every few minutes. Identical GET requests hammer the Lambda backend thousands of times per minute. What reduces backend load with minimal changes?
options: Enable API Gateway caching on the stage with a TTL of a few minutes
Raise the Lambda reserved concurrency
Move the API to a larger Lambda memory size
Switch the integration from Lambda to EC2
answer: Enable API Gateway caching on the stage with a TTL of a few minutes
explanation: Stage-level caching stores responses keyed by request (configurable per method and by parameters), serving repeats from cache until the TTL expires — the Lambda invocation count collapses, which also cuts cost. Matching the TTL to the data's change cadence (a few minutes) keeps staleness acceptable. More concurrency or memory just processes the redundant invocations faster; changing compute doesn't remove the redundancy.

question: A data-processing job needs scratch space with millions of IOPS and microsecond latency for temporary intermediate files that are worthless after the job completes. Which storage offers the highest performance for this?
options: NVMe instance store volumes on a storage-optimized instance family
An io2 EBS volume with maximum provisioned IOPS
Amazon EFS with provisioned throughput
Amazon S3 with multipart uploads
answer: NVMe instance store volumes on a storage-optimized instance family
explanation: Instance store is physically attached NVMe — no network hop — delivering millions of IOPS and microsecond latency that even io2 Block Express (network-attached) can't match. Its catch is ephemerality: data is lost on stop/termination, which is exactly acceptable for scratch files. The exam pattern: "temporary/scratch/cache + extreme IOPS" → instance store; "persistent + high IOPS" → io2.

question: An application caches database results in ElastiCache using lazy loading (cache-aside) only. Users complain that data is sometimes stale for a long time after updates. Adding which caching strategy keeps the cache current while preserving fast reads?
options: Write-through — update the cache at the same time the database is written
A shorter connection timeout to the cache
Caching the misses as well as the hits
Switching from Redis to Memcached
answer: Write-through — update the cache at the same time the database is written
explanation: Lazy loading populates the cache only on read misses, so an updated row stays stale until its cached copy expires. Write-through complements it: every database write also updates the cache, so reads always see current data. The classic combination is write-through plus lazy loading with a TTL as a safety net — TTLs bound staleness for anything written by paths that bypass the cache. The other options change failure behavior, memory usage, or engine, not freshness.

question: A new application's DynamoDB traffic is completely unpredictable — hours of near-zero activity, then sudden unannounced spikes. Which capacity mode is MOST cost-effective and operationally simple?
options: On-demand capacity mode — pay per request with no capacity planning
Provisioned capacity sized for the largest possible spike
Provisioned capacity with auto scaling and aggressive targets
Reserved capacity purchased for three years
answer: On-demand capacity mode — pay per request with no capacity planning
explanation: On-demand bills per million requests and absorbs sudden spikes without pre-provisioning — near-zero idle hours cost near zero. Provisioning for peak pays for the spike 24/7; auto scaling reacts in minutes, so unannounced spikes throttle first; reserved capacity commits to a baseline this workload doesn't have. The crossover: steady, predictable traffic eventually makes provisioned cheaper — the exam tests recognizing which side you're on.

question: An S3 bill shows significant storage charges that don't match the visible objects in the bucket. The bucket receives many large uploads from unreliable clients. What hidden cost is likely, and how is it fixed?
options: Abandoned incomplete multipart uploads — add a lifecycle rule with AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload
Delete markers from versioning — disable versioning
S3 access logs stored in the same bucket — disable logging
Cross-Region replication copies — delete the replica bucket
answer: Abandoned incomplete multipart uploads — add a lifecycle rule with AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload
explanation: Parts of a multipart upload that's never completed or aborted sit invisibly — they don't appear in object listings but bill as storage indefinitely. Unreliable clients abandoning large uploads accumulate them fast. The lifecycle rule `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` (e.g. after 7 days) cleans them automatically; Storage Lens and `ListMultipartUploads` reveal the backlog. The other options describe costs that are visible or intentional.

question: A containerized Linux workload runs on m5 (x86) instances. The team wants better price-performance with minimal changes. Which option typically delivers up to ~40% better price-performance?
options: Migrate to Graviton (ARM-based) instances such as m7g after rebuilding images for arm64
Upgrade to the newest x86 generation at the same size
Move every workload to t3.micro instances
Switch the containers to Windows hosts
answer: Migrate to Graviton (ARM-based) instances such as m7g after rebuilding images for arm64
explanation: Graviton instances are AWS's headline price-performance lever — up to 40% better than comparable x86 — and containerized Linux workloads are the easiest migration: rebuild multi-arch images, redeploy. Newer x86 generations help single-digit percentages; t3.micro is a size, not a strategy (undersizing causes throttling); Windows adds license cost. Watch for the constraint in questions: closed-source x86-only binaries block the move.

question: A development VPC has private subnets in three AZs, each with its own NAT gateway. The dev workloads tolerate downtime. What reduces NAT costs?
options: Consolidate to a single NAT gateway shared by all three AZs, accepting the availability trade-off
Replace the NAT gateways with internet gateways in each private subnet
Add a fourth NAT gateway for redundancy
Move all workloads to public subnets with public IPs
answer: Consolidate to a single NAT gateway shared by all three AZs, accepting the availability trade-off
explanation: Each NAT gateway bills hourly (~$32/month) plus per-GB processing; three of them triple the hourly cost. Dev environments that tolerate downtime can route all private subnets to one NAT gateway — the documented cost optimization, with the explicit trade-off that an AZ failure breaks egress for the others (which is why production keeps one per AZ, plus avoiding cross-AZ data charges). Internet gateways don't provide NAT for private instances; public IPs change the security posture.

question: A popular site serves large downloads directly from S3 to the internet, generating big data-transfer-out charges. How can delivery cost be reduced while improving download speed?
options: Serve the downloads through CloudFront — S3-to-CloudFront transfer is free and edge delivery rates are lower
Compress all files into ZIP archives
Move the bucket to a cheaper Region and keep serving directly
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for the downloads
answer: Serve the downloads through CloudFront — S3-to-CloudFront transfer is free and edge delivery rates are lower
explanation: Origin-to-CloudFront transfer is free, CloudFront's per-GB internet rates undercut S3's, caching means popular files leave the origin once instead of millions of times, and users download from nearby edges — cheaper *and* faster. Compression helps but doesn't change rates; Region arbitrage saves cents while adding latency; Transfer Acceleration is for *uploads* and adds cost.

question: A high-volume Lambda function dominates the monthly serverless bill. The code is already efficient. Which combination of changes reduces its cost without rewriting the logic? (Select TWO)
options: Migrate the function to arm64 (Graviton), which is billed about 20% cheaper per ms
Tune the memory setting to the sweet spot using power tuning, since billing is memory × duration
Increase the timeout to the 15-minute maximum
Switch the function to provisioned concurrency at all hours
Invoke the function more frequently with smaller payloads
answers: Migrate the function to arm64 (Graviton), which is billed about 20% cheaper per ms
Tune the memory setting to the sweet spot using power tuning, since billing is memory × duration
explanation: Lambda bills GB-seconds: arm64 cuts the per-ms price (~20%) and often runs faster too, while memory tuning finds the point where added CPU shortens duration enough to lower memory × time (tools like Lambda Power Tuning automate the sweep — sometimes *more* memory is cheaper). Timeout is a safety cap, not a billing factor; always-on provisioned concurrency *adds* an hourly charge; more invocations means more request fees and per-invocation overhead.

question: A company must restore 500 TB from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval for a regulatory review due in one week. Cost matters more than speed. Which retrieval option should they use?
options: Bulk retrieval — the cheapest tier, completing within 5–12 hours
Expedited retrieval for every archive
Standard retrieval with provisioned capacity units
Copy the archives to S3 Standard first, then download
answer: Bulk retrieval — the cheapest tier, completing within 5–12 hours
explanation: Glacier Flexible Retrieval offers three tiers: expedited (1–5 min, most expensive), standard (3–5 h), and bulk (5–12 h, lowest cost — designed exactly for large planned restores like this). A week of lead time makes bulk's window irrelevant. Expedited at 500 TB maximizes spend for unneeded speed; provisioned capacity exists to guarantee *expedited* throughput; "copy first" still performs a retrieval underneath.

question: Internal tools average 5% CPU with occasional brief bursts to 60%. They currently run on m5.large instances. Which instance family is designed for this usage pattern at lower cost?
options: T family burstable instances (e.g. t3.large), which accrue CPU credits while idle and spend them during bursts
C family compute-optimized instances
R family memory-optimized instances
P family GPU instances
answer: T family burstable instances (e.g. t3.large), which accrue CPU credits while idle and spend them during bursts
explanation: Burstable instances price for a low CPU baseline and bank credits during idle time to spend on bursts — a 5%-average workload runs comfortably and costs notably less than the equivalent m5. Watch the failure mode (also exam-tested): sustained high CPU drains credits and throttles to baseline, unless `unlimited` mode is on — which can quietly cost more than a fixed-performance instance.

question: A fault-tolerant processing fleet runs on Spot Instances of a single instance type and suffers frequent simultaneous interruptions when that capacity pool gets reclaimed. What reduces both interruptions and cost?
options: Use an Auto Scaling group with a mixed instances policy diversifying across many instance types and AZs, with the capacity-optimized allocation strategy
Bid a higher maximum price for the same single instance type
Switch the whole fleet to On-Demand
Run all Spot instances in one AZ to keep them together
answer: Use an Auto Scaling group with a mixed instances policy diversifying across many instance types and AZs, with the capacity-optimized allocation strategy
explanation: Spot interruptions happen per capacity pool (instance type × AZ). Diversifying across many pools means a single pool's reclamation takes out only a slice of the fleet, and the capacity-optimized strategy launches into the deepest pools, statistically reducing interruptions. "Bidding" higher doesn't help — the strategy is capacity-driven, and you pay the Spot market price regardless. Full On-Demand forfeits the ~90% savings; concentrating in one AZ is maximum blast radius.

question: Thousands of EBS snapshots accumulate from years of ad-hoc backups, inflating storage costs. The policy should be: daily snapshots, retain 14 days, then delete — automatically. Which service implements this?
options: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) snapshot policies
A reminder for engineers to clean up monthly
S3 lifecycle rules applied to the snapshots
AWS Trusted Advisor automated deletion
answer: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) snapshot policies
explanation: DLM automates EBS snapshot (and AMI) lifecycles: tag-targeted policies create snapshots on schedule and expire them by age or count — exactly "daily, keep 14, delete". (AWS Backup is the broader alternative when one plan must span multiple services.) S3 lifecycle rules don't govern EBS snapshots even though snapshots live in S3 internally; Trusted Advisor reports, it doesn't delete; manual cleanup is how the problem grew.

question: A monthly cost review should automatically surface idle and underused resources — unattached EBS volumes, idle load balancers, underutilized EC2 instances — with concrete recommendations. Which TWO tools provide these findings? (Select TWO)
options: AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks
AWS Compute Optimizer rightsizing recommendations
AWS CloudTrail event history
Amazon Route 53 health checks
AWS Artifact reports
answers: AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks
AWS Compute Optimizer rightsizing recommendations
explanation: Trusted Advisor's cost checks flag idle resources — unassociated Elastic IPs, idle load balancers, low-utilization instances, unattached volumes. Compute Optimizer goes deeper on sizing: ML over CloudWatch metrics yields specific instance-type recommendations (also for EBS, Lambda, ECS). Together they cover "what's wasted" and "what's oversized". CloudTrail is an API audit log; Route 53 checks endpoint health; Artifact downloads compliance documents.

question: Non-production RDS instances (dev, test, staging) run 24/7 but are only used during business hours on weekdays. Snapshots must be retained. What is the simplest cost reduction?
options: Stop the instances outside business hours (e.g. with an automated scheduler), since stopped instances don't incur instance-hours
Delete the instances every evening and recreate them each morning from scratch
Convert them all to Multi-AZ for efficiency
Move them to io2 storage
answer: Stop the instances outside business hours (e.g. with an automated scheduler), since stopped instances don't incur instance-hours
explanation: Stopped RDS instances stop billing instance-hours (storage and backups still bill) — nights and weekends cut runtime ~75%. Caveat worth knowing: RDS auto-starts stopped instances after 7 days, so schedulers re-stop them. Delete/recreate loses configuration and takes time daily; Multi-AZ *doubles* instance cost; io2 raises storage cost. Pair with right-sizing for the remaining hours.

question: A security review flags that a web application with an SSRF vulnerability could be tricked into reading EC2 instance credentials from the instance metadata service. Which configuration mitigates this class of attack?
options: Require IMDSv2 by setting HttpTokens to required in the instances' metadata options
Remove the IAM role from the instances entirely
Block the 169.254.169.254 address in the VPC's network ACLs
Enable detailed monitoring on the instances
answer: Require IMDSv2 by setting HttpTokens to required in the instances' metadata options
explanation: IMDSv2 makes metadata access session-oriented: callers must first obtain a token via a PUT request with a special header — something a typical SSRF forward of a GET request can't do. Enforcing it (HttpTokens=required) shuts down the classic credential-theft path. Removing the role breaks legitimate AWS access; NACLs don't filter the instance's own link-local metadata traffic; monitoring observes rather than prevents.

question: A compliance policy requires the KMS customer managed key encrypting a data lake to have its cryptographic material rotated every year, without re-encrypting existing data or changing key ARNs in applications. How is this done?
options: Enable automatic key rotation on the customer managed key
Create a new key every year and update every application
Export the key material annually and re-import a new version
Delete and recreate the key each January
answer: Enable automatic key rotation on the customer managed key
explanation: Automatic rotation generates fresh backing material on schedule (yearly by default) while the key ID, ARN, policies, and grants stay identical — KMS keeps the old material to decrypt data encrypted under it, so nothing needs re-encryption and applications notice nothing. Manual key creation forces application updates; imported key material actually *excludes* automatic rotation; deletion destroys the ability to decrypt existing data.

question: A financial institution's policy requires encryption keys to be stored in a single-tenant hardware security module validated to FIPS 140-2 Level 3, with the institution holding exclusive control of the HSM. Which service meets this requirement?
options: AWS CloudHSM
AWS KMS with customer managed keys
AWS Secrets Manager
AWS Certificate Manager
answer: AWS CloudHSM
explanation: CloudHSM provisions dedicated, single-tenant HSMs in your VPC, validated at FIPS 140-2 Level 3, where AWS has no access to your keys — you manage users and crypto operations directly (and can even use it as a KMS custom key store). Standard KMS is multi-tenant managed infrastructure; the "single-tenant + Level 3 + exclusive control" phrasing is the exam's signal for CloudHSM. Secrets Manager stores secrets, not HSMs; ACM manages TLS certificates.

question: A security team must continuously scan EC2 instances and ECR container images for software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and unintended network exposure, with findings ranked by severity. Which service does this?
options: Amazon Inspector
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Config
Amazon Macie
answer: Amazon Inspector
explanation: Inspector is the vulnerability scanner: it continuously assesses EC2 (via the SSM agent), ECR images, and Lambda functions against CVE databases and checks network reachability, producing risk-scored findings. The distinction the exam tests: GuardDuty detects active *threats* from log analysis; Inspector finds *vulnerabilities* before exploitation; Macie classifies sensitive data; Config checks configuration compliance.

question: A company runs GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie across 40 accounts. Security wants ONE place that aggregates all findings, runs automated checks against standards like CIS AWS Foundations, and shows a consolidated security score. Which service provides this?
options: AWS Security Hub
AWS CloudTrail
Amazon Detective
AWS Systems Manager
answer: AWS Security Hub
explanation: Security Hub is the aggregation layer: it ingests findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Access Analyzer, and partner tools across accounts (organization integration), normalizes them into one format, and continuously evaluates security standards (CIS, AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, PCI DSS) with scores. CloudTrail is raw API logging; Detective is for investigating specific findings more deeply; Systems Manager is operations tooling.

question: A regulated company must inspect and filter ALL traffic leaving its VPCs — including blocking outbound requests to unapproved domains and applying intrusion-prevention signatures — using a managed AWS service. Which fits?
options: AWS Network Firewall deployed at the VPC perimeter
Security groups with outbound rules
AWS WAF on an internet-facing ALB
Amazon GuardDuty
answer: AWS Network Firewall deployed at the VPC perimeter
explanation: Network Firewall is the managed network-layer firewall: stateful rules, FQDN/domain filtering for egress, and Suricata-compatible IDS/IPS signatures, scaling automatically at VPC boundaries. Security groups allow/deny by port and CIDR — no domain names or signatures, and no deny logging. WAF inspects *inbound* HTTP to your web endpoints, not general egress; GuardDuty detects (including DNS exfiltration) but doesn't block.

question: Remote employees need secure access to applications in private subnets from their laptops anywhere in the world, using standard OpenVPN-based clients — without exposing the applications publicly. Which managed service provides this?
options: AWS Client VPN
AWS Site-to-Site VPN
AWS Direct Connect
Amazon Connect
answer: AWS Client VPN
explanation: Client VPN is the managed remote-access VPN: individual users connect with OpenVPN-based clients to a Client VPN endpoint, authenticate (Active Directory, SAML, or certificates), and reach VPC and on-premises resources per authorization rules — elastic, no VPN servers to run. Site-to-Site VPN connects *networks* (office to VPC), not roaming laptops; Direct Connect is a physical circuit; Amazon Connect is a contact-center product (a name-trap distractor).

question: A company connects its data center to AWS via Direct Connect. A new compliance rule requires ALL traffic over the link to be encrypted in transit. Direct Connect does not encrypt by default. What is the standard solution?
options: Run an AWS Site-to-Site VPN over the Direct Connect connection
Nothing — Direct Connect is private, which satisfies encryption requirements
Replace Direct Connect with a faster internet connection
Enable encryption on the Direct Connect virtual interface checkbox
answer: Run an AWS Site-to-Site VPN over the Direct Connect connection
explanation: Direct Connect provides private, dedicated connectivity — but the bits are not encrypted. Layering an IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over a public virtual interface gives encryption in transit while keeping DX's consistent bandwidth and latency (MACsec is the alternative on supported 10/100 Gbps ports). "Private" and "encrypted" are different claims — a distinction the exam tests directly. There is no encryption checkbox on a VIF.

question: A mobile app authenticates users with a Cognito user pool. After login, the app must upload photos DIRECTLY to an S3 bucket — without routing the bytes through a backend server, and without embedding AWS credentials in the app. What enables this?
options: A Cognito identity pool that exchanges the user pool token for temporary, scoped AWS credentials
An IAM user access key shipped in the app binary, obfuscated
Making the S3 bucket publicly writable for authenticated app versions
Cognito user pool groups with S3 permissions attached directly
answer: A Cognito identity pool that exchanges the user pool token for temporary, scoped AWS credentials
explanation: This is the user pools vs identity pools division: user pools *authenticate* (issue JWTs); identity pools *authorize against AWS* — they trade a valid token for temporary STS credentials tied to an IAM role, which can even scope S3 prefixes per user identity. Embedded keys are extractable from any binary; public-write buckets accept uploads from anyone; user pool groups map to roles only via an identity pool anyway.

question: A web application must let a customer download one specific private S3 object for the next 15 minutes, without changing bucket policies or making anything public. What should the backend generate?
options: An S3 presigned URL with a 15-minute expiry
A bucket policy granting the customer's IP access
A new IAM user for the customer
A public object ACL that a cleanup job removes later
answer: An S3 presigned URL with a 15-minute expiry
explanation: A presigned URL embeds a signature derived from the backend's own credentials, granting exactly one operation on one object until expiry — no policy changes, no public exposure, revoked by time. They work for uploads (PUT) too. Per-customer IP policies and IAM users are heavyweight and error-prone; temporarily-public ACLs are a breach window with a cleanup dependency.

question: After tightening a network ACL to allow only inbound port 443, clients can no longer receive responses from the web servers in that subnet — connections hang. Security groups are correct. What did the team forget?
options: An outbound NACL rule allowing ephemeral ports (1024–65535), since NACLs are stateless and response traffic is evaluated separately
An inbound rule for port 80
Enabling stateful mode on the network ACL
A route table entry for return traffic
answer: An outbound NACL rule allowing ephemeral ports (1024–65535), since NACLs are stateless and response traffic is evaluated separately
explanation: NACLs evaluate every packet in each direction independently — there is no connection tracking and no "stateful mode". A client connects *to* port 443 but receives responses on its ephemeral source port, so the subnet's outbound NACL must allow the ephemeral range. This stateless-return-traffic trap is among the most reliable exam questions on VPC networking. Routing isn't direction-specific per flow.

question: A security policy bans long-lived database passwords for applications connecting to RDS MySQL. Connections should authenticate using short-lived tokens tied to IAM identities instead. Which feature enables this?
options: IAM database authentication, generating 15-minute authentication tokens
Storing the password in an encrypted configuration file
Using the RDS master password for all applications
SSH key pairs configured on the DB instance
answer: IAM database authentication, generating 15-minute authentication tokens
explanation: IAM database authentication (RDS MySQL/MariaDB/PostgreSQL) lets a database user authenticate with a token generated from the caller's IAM credentials — valid 15 minutes, no password stored anywhere, access controlled and revoked through IAM, traffic forced over SSL. Encrypted config files still hold a long-lived secret; shared master passwords are the anti-pattern being banned; RDS instances don't take SSH keys.

question: An audit found several unencrypted EBS volumes created by developers who forgot to tick the encryption option. How can the company guarantee every NEW EBS volume in the Region is encrypted, regardless of how it's created?
options: Enable EBS encryption by default in the account settings for that Region
Send a reminder email to all developers
Run a weekly script that deletes unencrypted volumes
Require all volumes to be created by one admin
answer: Enable EBS encryption by default in the account settings for that Region
explanation: EBS encryption by default is a per-Region account setting: every new volume and snapshot copy is automatically encrypted with the chosen KMS key, no per-creation flags needed — console, CLI, API, and Auto Scaling launches all included. Reminders don't enforce; deletion scripts destroy data after the fact; centralizing creation is an operational bottleneck. (Existing unencrypted volumes still need the snapshot-copy migration.)

question: A developer accidentally committed an IAM user's access keys to a public GitHub repository. Which TWO actions should be taken immediately? (Select TWO)
options: Deactivate or delete the exposed access keys
Review CloudTrail for any API activity made with the exposed keys
Delete the GitHub repository and consider the incident closed
Rotate the account's root user password only
Wait to see whether AWS sends an abuse notification first
answers: Deactivate or delete the exposed access keys
Review CloudTrail for any API activity made with the exposed keys
explanation: Bots scan public repos for keys within minutes, so the order is: kill the credential immediately, then audit what it did — CloudTrail shows every call made with the key, revealing whether resources were created (crypto-mining EC2 is the classic), data accessed, or persistence established. Deleting the repo doesn't un-leak anything (forks, caches, scrapers); the root password is a different credential; waiting concedes the head start.

question: A REST API on Amazon API Gateway must (a) accept requests only from authenticated users of the company's existing Cognito user pool and (b) be protected against common web exploits like SQL injection. Which combination meets both requirements? (Select TWO)
options: Configure a Cognito user pool authorizer on the API's methods
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the API Gateway stage
Enable CORS on every resource
Issue long-lived API keys to each user
Move the API into a private subnet
answers: Configure a Cognito user pool authorizer on the API's methods
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the API Gateway stage
explanation: Two requirements, two controls: the Cognito authorizer validates the user pool's JWT on every request (authentication), and WAF filters exploit patterns like SQL injection before they reach the integration (protection). CORS is a browser policy, not security; API keys identify *clients for usage plans/throttling* — explicitly not an authentication mechanism; API Gateway endpoints don't live in your subnets (though private endpoint types exist, that addresses exposure, not these two requirements).

question: An application needs to store a few configuration secrets (an API key and a license string) encrypted at rest, retrieved at runtime by IAM-authorized roles. Automatic rotation is NOT required, and the team wants zero additional cost. Which service fits?
options: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with SecureString parameters
AWS Secrets Manager
A DynamoDB table with client-side encryption
Environment variables in plaintext
answer: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with SecureString parameters
explanation: Parameter Store standard parameters are free: SecureString values are KMS-encrypted, retrieved via IAM-controlled API calls, and versioned. Secrets Manager charges per secret per month — what it buys is managed rotation and cross-account access, which this scenario explicitly doesn't need. The exam frequently poses exactly this trade: rotation or cross-account → Secrets Manager; simple encrypted config at no cost → Parameter Store.

question: A network team manages a central VPC with subnets that several application accounts in the same AWS Organization should deploy resources into — without duplicating VPCs or peering. Which service enables sharing the subnets across accounts?
options: AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM)
VPC peering from each account
AWS Direct Connect gateway
IAM cross-account roles
answer: AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM)
explanation: RAM shares resources — VPC subnets, Transit Gateways, Route 53 Resolver rules, license configurations — with accounts or OUs in the organization. Shared-VPC participants launch resources into the shared subnets while the owner keeps network control: one VPC, centrally managed, no peering mesh or CIDR coordination. Peering connects *separate* VPCs; a DX gateway is for hybrid connectivity; IAM roles grant API access, not subnet placement.

question: A solutions architect is setting up an AWS Site-to-Site VPN between a corporate data center and a VPC. Which TWO components must be configured to establish the connection? (Select TWO)
options: A customer gateway representing the on-premises VPN device
A virtual private gateway (or transit gateway) attached on the AWS side
An internet gateway in the data center
A NAT gateway in the corporate network
AWS Direct Connect cross-connects
answers: A customer gateway representing the on-premises VPN device
A virtual private gateway (or transit gateway) attached on the AWS side
explanation: A Site-to-Site VPN is defined by its two endpoints: the customer gateway resource (the on-premises router's public IP and ASN) and the virtual private gateway attached to the VPC — or a transit gateway when connecting many VPCs. AWS then provisions two IPsec tunnels to distinct endpoints for HA. Internet/NAT gateways are VPC egress constructs, and cross-connects belong to Direct Connect, a different connectivity product.

question: A licensing-restricted application must run on exactly one EC2 instance (no Auto Scaling group allowed). If the underlying hardware fails, the instance should be brought back automatically — keeping its instance ID, private IP, and Elastic IP. What provides this?
options: EC2 automatic recovery via a CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System with the recover action
A second instance in another AZ behind an ALB
An hourly AMI backup with manual relaunch
EC2 Spot capacity rebalancing
answer: EC2 automatic recovery via a CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System with the recover action
explanation: Instance recovery migrates the instance to healthy hardware while preserving its identity — instance ID, private and Elastic IPs, metadata — perfect for license-bound singletons (newer instance types enable simplified automatic recovery by default). The recover action handles *system* status failures (host issues); a second instance violates the constraint; manual relaunch means downtime and a new identity; capacity rebalancing is a Spot feature.

question: When an Auto Scaling group scales in, terminated instances lose in-memory job state and unshipped log files. The team needs a window to drain work and upload logs BEFORE each instance is terminated. Which feature provides this?
options: A termination lifecycle hook that pauses the instance in Terminating:Wait while a script finishes cleanup
Suspending the Terminate process on the ASG permanently
A larger health check grace period
Scale-in protection on every instance forever
answer: A termination lifecycle hook that pauses the instance in Terminating:Wait while a script finishes cleanup
explanation: Lifecycle hooks pause the instance between "selected for termination" and "terminated": the hook fires a notification (EventBridge/SNS/SQS), your script drains jobs and ships logs, then calls complete-lifecycle-action (or the timeout elapses). Launch hooks exist symmetrically for warm-up. Suspending Terminate or protecting every instance breaks scale-in entirely; grace periods govern health evaluation after *launch*.

question: During deployments, users see errors as instances are removed from an ALB target group while still processing in-flight requests. Which setting lets active requests finish before an instance is fully removed?
options: The target group's deregistration delay (connection draining)
A longer ALB idle timeout
Sticky sessions on the target group
Cross-zone load balancing
answer: The target group's deregistration delay (connection draining)
explanation: When a target deregisters, the ALB immediately stops sending it NEW requests but keeps existing connections alive for the deregistration delay (default 300 s) so in-flight requests complete. Tuning it to the longest expected request eliminates deployment errors. Idle timeout closes inactive connections; stickiness pins users to instances (making removal *worse*); cross-zone is about distribution, not draining.

question: An application takes 4 minutes to initialize after instance launch. The Auto Scaling group keeps terminating brand-new instances as unhealthy before they finish booting, looping forever. Which setting fixes this?
options: Increase the ASG health check grace period beyond the initialization time
Disable health checks entirely
Reduce the ALB health check interval
Set the ASG cooldown to zero
answer: Increase the ASG health check grace period beyond the initialization time
explanation: The grace period tells the ASG how long to ignore health check results after launch, giving slow-booting applications time to come up. Set below the real init time, every instance is judged before it's ready, terminated, and replaced — a continuous churn loop. Disabling checks removes self-healing; a *faster* ALB interval makes the judgment come sooner; cooldown spacing doesn't change health evaluation.

question: A DynamoDB table must be protected so it can be restored to ANY point in the last 35 days after accidental writes or deletes. Which feature should be enabled?
options: Point-in-time recovery (PITR)
DynamoDB Streams
Global tables
DynamoDB Accelerator
answer: Point-in-time recovery (PITR)
explanation: PITR maintains continuous backups, restorable to any second in the preceding 35 days — into a new table, from which data is recovered. On-demand backups complement it for long-term snapshots. Streams capture change events (great for triggers, not a restore mechanism); global tables replicate corruption faithfully across Regions; DAX is a cache. "Restore to any point in time" → PITR is direct exam vocabulary.

question: A company's shared EFS file system is critical, and DR planning requires a copy in another Region kept current automatically, with failover possible in minutes. Which feature meets this?
options: EFS replication to a file system in the second Region
Nightly rsync from an EC2 instance to the other Region
EBS snapshots copied cross-Region
Mounting the same EFS file system from the second Region
answer: EFS replication to a file system in the second Region
explanation: EFS replication continuously replicates the file system to another Region (or AZ) with an RPO/RTO of minutes — managed, no agents or sync jobs. For failover, replication is stopped and the replica becomes writable. Hand-rolled rsync is operational toil with hours of RPO; EBS snapshots don't apply to EFS; EFS mount targets exist only within the file system's own Region (cross-Region NFS over peering is a latency trap, not DR).

question: A team wants DNS to return up to eight healthy IP addresses for their service, letting clients pick among them — with unhealthy endpoints automatically excluded — WITHOUT the cost of a load balancer. Which Route 53 routing policy does this?
options: Multivalue answer routing with health checks
Simple routing with multiple values in one record
Failover routing
Weighted routing at 100/0
answer: Multivalue answer routing with health checks
explanation: Multivalue answer routing returns up to eight records, each individually health-checked — unhealthy IPs drop out of responses, and clients spread across the rest. It's DNS-level pseudo-load-balancing: cheaper than an ELB but without connection awareness, draining, or instant failover (DNS TTL caching applies). Simple records with multiple values can't attach health checks per value; failover is active-passive; weighted 100/0 sends everything to one target.

question: After an order is placed, a confirmation job must NOT be processed for at least 10 minutes (to allow cancellations) before workers consume it from SQS. Which feature implements the delay?
options: A delay queue (or per-message timers) postponing delivery up to 15 minutes
A visibility timeout of 10 minutes
Long polling with a 10-minute wait
A FIFO queue, which processes in timed order
answer: A delay queue (or per-message timers) postponing delivery up to 15 minutes
explanation: Delay queues (DelaySeconds on the queue) and per-message timers hide a message from consumers for up to 15 minutes *from when it's sent* — exactly "don't process before X". Visibility timeout hides a message *after it's received*, governing retry windows, not initial delay — the exam's favorite confusion pair here. Long polling waits at most 20 seconds; FIFO orders messages but doesn't delay them.

question: A company's primary connection to AWS is a Direct Connect link carrying business-critical traffic. The architect must add a cost-effective failover path in case the DX circuit fails. What is the recommended design?
options: An AWS Site-to-Site VPN over the internet as a standby for the Direct Connect connection
A second identical Direct Connect circuit from the same provider through the same location
Nothing — Direct Connect has built-in redundancy
An S3 Transfer Acceleration endpoint
answer: An AWS Site-to-Site VPN over the internet as a standby for the Direct Connect connection
explanation: DX + VPN backup is the documented cost-effective resilience pattern: BGP prefers the DX path while it's healthy, and routing fails over to the IPsec VPN when the circuit drops — lower bandwidth, but connectivity survives. A second DX through the same location/provider shares failure modes (and costs far more — appropriate when bandwidth must survive too, via separate locations); a single DX has no built-in redundancy; Transfer Acceleration is an S3 upload feature.

question: A team wants to release a new application version with the ability to shift a small percentage of live traffic to it, observe error rates, then either continue shifting or roll back instantly. Which combination implements this on an ALB-based architecture? (Select TWO)
options: Deploy the new version to a separate target group (green) alongside the current one (blue)
Use ALB weighted target groups to shift traffic gradually between blue and green
Replace the instances in the existing target group one by one with the new version
Lower the ALB health check thresholds during the deployment
Shift traffic by changing instance sizes in the existing group
answers: Deploy the new version to a separate target group (green) alongside the current one (blue)
Use ALB weighted target groups to shift traffic gradually between blue and green
explanation: Blue/green with canary shifting needs two independently routable environments: the green target group runs the new version, and the ALB listener rule's weights move traffic 1% → 10% → 100% (or back to 0% instantly on errors — the rollback is a weight change, not a redeploy). In-place instance replacement has no rollback path and mixes versions in one pool; health thresholds and instance sizes don't direct traffic between versions.

question: Messages in an SQS queue must be processed by Lambda, scaling consumers automatically with queue depth, batching messages, and returning failures to the queue — with no polling infrastructure to manage. What connects the queue to the function?
options: An event source mapping from the SQS queue to the Lambda function
A cron-scheduled Lambda that polls the queue every minute
An SNS topic between the queue and the function
An EC2 poller fleet invoking Lambda via the SDK
answer: An event source mapping from the SQS queue to the Lambda function
explanation: The event source mapping is Lambda's managed poller: it long-polls the queue, invokes the function with batches, scales pollers up and down with traffic, and leaves failed batches (or items, with partial batch responses) to reappear for retry per the queue's redrive policy. Scheduled polling adds latency and fixed cadence; SNS inverts the pattern and drops the buffering; an EC2 poller fleet is exactly the infrastructure this feature eliminates.

question: A small team runs containers and wants AWS to handle servers entirely: no EC2 instances to patch or scale, tasks restarted automatically if they fail, and a service keeping the desired task count running. Which combination provides this?
options: Amazon ECS services on AWS Fargate
Amazon ECS on self-managed EC2 container instances
Docker installed on a single large EC2 instance
AWS Lambda functions only
answer: Amazon ECS services on AWS Fargate
explanation: Fargate is serverless container compute — no instances exist for the team to patch, size, or scale — and an ECS *service* adds the resilience contract: it monitors tasks, replaces failures, maintains desired count across AZs, and integrates load balancer health checks. The EC2 launch type reintroduces fleet management; one big Docker host is a single point of failure; Lambda suits functions, not arbitrary long-running containers.

question: A company patches its long-lived EC2 fleet in place over SSH, and configuration drift keeps causing mysterious incidents. Which practice eliminates drift by design?
options: Immutable infrastructure — bake a new AMI per change and roll it out by replacing instances (e.g. ASG instance refresh)
A stricter change-approval process for SSH sessions
Larger instances so changes are needed less often
Manual configuration audits every quarter
answer: Immutable infrastructure — bake a new AMI per change and roll it out by replacing instances (e.g. ASG instance refresh)
explanation: Immutable infrastructure forbids modifying running servers: every change produces a new artifact (AMI/launch template version), and deployment means replacing instances — ASG instance refresh rolls the fleet gradually with health checks. Drift becomes impossible (servers are reproducible from the artifact) and rollback is redeploying the previous version. Process and audits manage drift; immutability removes its mechanism. The exam guide lists this under resilient design.

question: A production RDS database was nearly deleted by a mistaken script last month. Which TWO configurations protect against losing the database and its data this way? (Select TWO)
options: Enable deletion protection on the DB instance
Enable automated backups with an appropriate retention period
Disable Multi-AZ to simplify the setup
Grant all engineers rds:DeleteDBInstance for accountability
Turn off final snapshots to speed up operations
answers: Enable deletion protection on the DB instance
Enable automated backups with an appropriate retention period
explanation: Defense in depth: deletion protection makes `DeleteDBInstance` fail outright until the flag is deliberately removed (a separate, conscious step), and automated backups guarantee point-in-time recovery if data is ever lost anyway. The distractors actively reduce safety — wider delete permissions, no final snapshot, less redundancy. IAM least privilege on delete actions is the complementary control.

question: A backend service is overwhelmed when API clients send sudden bursts far beyond its capacity. The team wants API Gateway to reject excess requests with HTTP 429 before they reach the backend, with different limits per API consumer. What should they configure?
options: Throttling limits with usage plans and API keys per consumer
A larger backend so throttling is unnecessary
Client-side rate limiting guidelines in the documentation
An SQS queue inside API Gateway
answer: Throttling limits with usage plans and API keys per consumer
explanation: API Gateway throttles with a token-bucket (rate + burst) at account, stage, method, and — via usage plans with API keys — per-consumer levels, returning 429 Too Many Requests when exceeded. The backend only ever sees traffic within the contract, and noisy clients can't starve others. Over-provisioning pays for abuse; documentation isn't enforcement; API Gateway doesn't embed queues (that's a separate integration pattern).

question: An Aurora cluster has a writer and two replicas. If the writer instance fails, what happens?
options: Aurora automatically promotes a replica to writer (typically in under 30 seconds), following the configured failover priority tiers
The cluster is read-only until an administrator restores the writer from a snapshot
All data since the last backup is lost
The cluster endpoint must be manually repointed to a replica
answer: Aurora automatically promotes a replica to writer (typically in under 30 seconds), following the configured failover priority tiers
explanation: Aurora replicas share the same distributed storage volume as the writer, so promotion needs no data copying — failover typically completes in under 30 seconds, choosing the candidate by priority tier (0–15, lower first, then largest instance). The cluster endpoint follows the new writer automatically; applications just reconnect. No storage-level data is lost (six copies across three AZs). With *no* replica, Aurora instead recreates the writer, which is slower.

question: A company has 60 VPCs across several accounts plus a Direct Connect link to its data center. Managing full-mesh VPC peering has become unmanageable. Which service consolidates this into a hub-and-spoke network?
options: AWS Transit Gateway
More VPC peering connections, organized in a spreadsheet
AWS PrivateLink between every VPC pair
A shared NAT gateway
answer: AWS Transit Gateway
explanation: Transit Gateway is the regional network hub: VPCs, VPN connections, and Direct Connect gateways attach once, and route tables on the hub control who reaches whom — thousands of attachments, with cross-Region peering available. A 60-VPC full mesh needs ~1,770 peering connections, and peering isn't transitive, which is exactly the wall this team hit. PrivateLink exposes specific *services*, not networks; NAT is internet egress.

question: A company transfers large datasets daily between its data center and AWS. The internet VPN's bandwidth fluctuates unpredictably, breaking transfer deadlines. Which option provides consistent, dedicated network performance?
options: AWS Direct Connect
A second internet VPN tunnel
S3 Transfer Acceleration
Larger EC2 instances at the AWS end
answer: AWS Direct Connect
explanation: Direct Connect is a dedicated physical circuit (1/10/100 Gbps, or hosted capacities) between the data center and AWS — bandwidth and latency are consistent because the traffic never crosses the public internet. VPNs ride the internet, so a second tunnel inherits the same variability. Transfer Acceleration helps S3 uploads over the internet but guarantees nothing; receiving-side instance size doesn't fix the pipe.

question: A site on CloudFront runs A/B tests: based on a cookie, requests must be routed to one of two different origins. The logic must run at the edge with no round trip to a Region. Which feature implements this?
options: Lambda@Edge on the origin request event, rewriting the origin based on the cookie
CloudFront geographic restrictions
Route 53 weighted routing
An S3 redirect rule
answer: Lambda@Edge on the origin request event, rewriting the origin based on the cookie
explanation: Lambda@Edge runs functions at CloudFront locations on viewer/origin request and response events — origin-request functions can inspect cookies and change the origin per request, the canonical A/B mechanism. CloudFront Functions are the lighter, cheaper sibling for sub-millisecond header/URL rewrites on viewer events, but origin selection lives with Lambda@Edge. Geo restrictions block countries; Route 53 weights split by DNS query, blind to cookies; S3 redirects can't read them either.

question: A data team runs nightly Apache Spark jobs processing terabytes from S3, wanting cluster management handled by AWS and the ability to use Spot Instances for the worker fleet. Which service fits?
options: Amazon EMR
AWS Lambda
Amazon RDS
Amazon QuickSight
answer: Amazon EMR
explanation: EMR is managed big-data infrastructure: provisioned clusters running Spark, Hadoop, Hive, and Presto, reading straight from S3 (EMRFS), with deep Spot integration for task nodes — transient clusters that exist only for the nightly run are the cost-efficient pattern. Lambda caps at 15 minutes and 10 GB — wrong shape for terabyte Spark jobs; RDS is a relational database; QuickSight visualizes results rather than computing them.

question: A genomics company runs hundreds of thousands of containerized analysis jobs with varying CPU/memory needs and inter-job dependencies. They want managed job queues, automatic provisioning of right-sized compute, and Spot support — without building a scheduler. Which service?
options: AWS Batch
AWS Step Functions alone
Amazon SQS with manual workers
AWS Lambda
answer: AWS Batch
explanation: Batch is purpose-built batch scheduling: job definitions, priority queues, dependencies, array jobs for massive parallelism, and compute environments that provision optimal EC2/Spot/Fargate capacity per the queue's demands. Step Functions orchestrates workflows (and often *submits* Batch jobs) but isn't a batch scheduler with queues and packing; SQS+workers means building Batch yourself; Lambda's 15-minute/10 GB limits don't fit heavy analysis jobs.

question: Business analysts need interactive dashboards over data in Athena and Redshift, shareable with hundreds of users, with ML-powered insights — and no BI servers to manage. Which AWS service provides this?
options: Amazon QuickSight
Amazon CloudWatch dashboards
AWS Glue DataBrew
Amazon OpenSearch Dashboards
answer: Amazon QuickSight
explanation: QuickSight is the serverless BI service: native connectors to Athena, Redshift, RDS and S3, the in-memory SPICE engine for fast interactive queries, per-session pricing for readers, embedding, and ML insights like anomaly detection. CloudWatch dashboards visualize *metrics*; DataBrew is data preparation; OpenSearch Dashboards serves log/search analytics on OpenSearch data. The exam guide names QuickSight for visualization explicitly.

question: A social platform must answer queries like "friends of my friends who like hiking" across billions of relationships in milliseconds. Relational JOINs have become unusably slow. Which purpose-built database fits?
options: Amazon Neptune
Amazon Redshift
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon ElastiCache
answer: Amazon Neptune
explanation: Neptune is the managed graph database — property graphs (Gremlin/openCypher) and RDF (SPARQL) — built to traverse relationship networks in milliseconds where the equivalent SQL needs explosive self-JOINs. Social graphs, recommendations, fraud rings, and knowledge graphs are its signature scenarios. Redshift aggregates columns, DynamoDB serves key-value at scale, ElastiCache caches — none traverse relationships natively.

question: A database on a c5.large instance uses an io2 volume provisioned with 40,000 IOPS, but CloudWatch shows the volume never exceeds ~20,000 IOPS while the application is I/O starved. The volume metrics show no queue saturation. What is the likely bottleneck?
options: The instance type's own EBS bandwidth/IOPS limit — a larger or storage-optimized instance is needed to drive the provisioned IOPS
io2 volumes cannot exceed 20,000 IOPS
The volume needs to be striped with RAID 1
EBS Multi-Attach must be enabled first
answer: The instance type's own EBS bandwidth/IOPS limit — a larger or storage-optimized instance is needed to drive the provisioned IOPS
explanation: EBS performance is min(volume, instance): every instance type has its own EBS-attached IOPS and throughput ceiling, and a c5.large caps far below 40,000 IOPS — the volume is fine, the instance can't push it. Scaling to a larger size (or an EBS-optimized-by-default family with higher EBS bandwidth) unlocks the provisioned performance. io2 goes to 64,000+; RAID 1 mirrors for redundancy (halving write throughput); Multi-Attach is about multiple instances, not speed.

question: A company's backup workflow writes to physical tape libraries, with software that expects an iSCSI virtual tape interface. They want to retire tape hardware and store backups in S3 and Glacier without changing the backup software. Which service fits?
options: AWS Storage Gateway — Tape Gateway
AWS Storage Gateway — File Gateway
AWS DataSync
Amazon EBS snapshots
answer: AWS Storage Gateway — Tape Gateway
explanation: Tape Gateway presents a virtual tape library (VTL) over iSCSI, so existing backup software (Veeam, NetBackup, Commvault) keeps working unchanged — virtual tapes land in S3 and "ejected" tapes archive to Glacier tiers. Mapping the Storage Gateway family is exam-core: File Gateway = NFS/SMB to S3, Volume Gateway = iSCSI block volumes, Tape Gateway = VTL. DataSync migrates files; EBS snapshots don't speak to backup software.

question: A research lab must move 600 TB of imagery to S3 within three weeks. Their site's internet uplink is 200 Mbps and cannot be upgraded. What should they use?
options: Multiple AWS Snowball Edge devices shipped to the site
AWS DataSync over the existing link
S3 Transfer Acceleration
Multipart uploads run 24/7
answer: Multiple AWS Snowball Edge devices shipped to the site
explanation: Do the math first — that's the exam skill: 600 TB over 200 Mbps ≈ 280+ days at full saturation; no online method (DataSync, Transfer Acceleration, multipart) beats the arithmetic of the pipe. Snowball Edge devices hold ~80 TB usable each; several in parallel, loaded locally and shipped back, complete the transfer within the deadline. Rule of thumb: when transfer time exceeds about a week of dedicated bandwidth, go offline.

question: An application downloads 10 GB files from S3 over high-bandwidth connections, but single-stream downloads are far slower than the available bandwidth, and a network blip restarts the whole file. What download strategy fixes both problems?
options: Parallel byte-range GET requests, each fetching a different part of the object
Switching the bucket to S3 One Zone-IA
Compressing the files into one larger archive
Downloading through a NAT gateway
answer: Parallel byte-range GET requests, each fetching a different part of the object
explanation: The `Range` header lets each request pull a slice of the object; running slices concurrently aggregates throughput far beyond one TCP stream, and a failed slice retries alone instead of restarting 10 GB. It's the download mirror of multipart upload (SDK transfer managers do both automatically). Storage class doesn't change wire speed; a bigger archive worsens the retry problem; NAT adds cost, not bandwidth.

question: An IoT platform ingests millions of sensor readings per minute, each with a timestamp. Queries are time-windowed aggregations ("average temperature per device over the last hour"), and old data should age out to cheaper storage automatically. Which purpose-built database fits?
options: Amazon Timestream
Amazon RDS PostgreSQL
Amazon Neptune
Amazon ElastiCache Redis
answer: Amazon Timestream
explanation: Timestream is the serverless time-series database: built for high-throughput timestamped ingestion, time-windowed SQL analytics (interpolation, smoothing), and automatic tiering from a memory store to a cheaper magnetic store by age. General-purpose RDS tables strain at this write rate and need hand-rolled partitioning/expiry; Neptune is graphs; Redis is a cache. "Sensor/metrics data + time-window queries" is the Timestream signature.

question: A web application served from us-east-1 has a growing user base in Asia and Australia complaining about slow page loads — both for static assets and for API calls. Which combination of changes improves their experience? (Select TWO)
options: Serve static assets through Amazon CloudFront
Deploy the application stack to an Asia-Pacific Region with Route 53 latency-based routing
Move the S3 assets to larger buckets
Increase the EC2 instance sizes in us-east-1
Switch the ALB in us-east-1 to a Network Load Balancer
answers: Serve static assets through Amazon CloudFront
Deploy the application stack to an Asia-Pacific Region with Route 53 latency-based routing
explanation: Distance is the enemy: CloudFront caches static content at edges near the users (and accelerates dynamic calls somewhat via backbone routing), while a second Regional deployment with latency routing puts the *API itself* close to them — attacking both halves of the complaint. Bucket "size" isn't a real dial; bigger instances and a different load balancer in Virginia don't shorten the 200+ ms round trip from Sydney.

question: An RDS database on gp2 storage performs well most of the day but slows dramatically during sustained heavy I/O periods. CloudWatch shows the volume's BurstBalance metric dropping to zero exactly when slowdowns start. What is happening, and what fixes it?
options: gp2 burst credits are exhausted, dropping IOPS to baseline — move to gp3 or Provisioned IOPS storage sized for the sustained load
The database needs more RAM — scale the instance class
Connections are leaking — add RDS Proxy
The storage is full — increase allocated capacity
answer: gp2 burst credits are exhausted, dropping IOPS to baseline — move to gp3 or Provisioned IOPS storage sized for the sustained load
explanation: gp2 earns burst credits at 3 IOPS/GB and spends them above baseline; sustained heavy I/O drains the bucket and performance collapses to baseline — the BurstBalance-hits-zero correlation is the textbook diagnosis. gp3 decouples performance from size with a flat 3,000 IOPS baseline (configurable higher); Provisioned IOPS suits the heaviest cases. RAM, connection pooling, and capacity are different problems with different metrics.

question: Medical images are written once and accessed about once per quarter, but when a doctor opens one it must load in milliseconds. Which storage class minimizes cost for this pattern?
options: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
S3 Standard
S3 Glacier Deep Archive
answer: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
