explanation: Glacier Instant Retrieval is the archive class with *millisecond* access — about 68% cheaper storage than Standard-IA for data touched roughly once a quarter, trading a higher per-GB retrieval fee that rare access keeps small. Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive take minutes to hours — fails the doctor's click; Standard pays full price for data that sits idle 99.9% of the time. "Rarely accessed but instant when needed" → Instant Retrieval.

question: A photo service stores thumbnails that are regenerated automatically from originals if ever lost. The thumbnails are accessed infrequently. Which storage class offers the LOWEST cost that still fits this data?
options: S3 One Zone-IA — cheaper because it forgoes multi-AZ resilience, acceptable for re-creatable data
S3 Standard-IA
S3 Standard
S3 Glacier Deep Archive
answer: S3 One Zone-IA — cheaper because it forgoes multi-AZ resilience, acceptable for re-creatable data
explanation: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ at ~20% less than Standard-IA. The trade-off — data loss if that AZ is destroyed — is precisely acceptable when the data is derivative and re-creatable (thumbnails, transcodes, replicas of on-prem data). That qualifier is the exam's cue; for primary or irreplaceable data, multi-AZ classes win. Deep Archive's hours-long retrieval doesn't suit serving images at all.

question: An EFS file system holds project files, most untouched for months, yet bills entirely at the Standard rate. Access patterns must not change for users. What reduces the cost?
options: Enable EFS lifecycle management to transition files not accessed for 30 days to EFS Infrequent Access
Move all files to instance store
Mount the file system read-only
Reduce the number of mount targets
answer: Enable EFS lifecycle management to transition files not accessed for 30 days to EFS Infrequent Access
explanation: EFS lifecycle management automatically moves files unaccessed for a configured window into EFS IA (up to ~92% cheaper per GB; an Archive class goes further), and transparently moves them back on access — same paths, same NFS semantics, users notice nothing but a slightly slower first read. Instance store is ephemeral local disk; read-only mounts and mount-target counts don't affect storage rates.

question: A DynamoDB table stores user sessions that are useless after 24 hours, but old items accumulate and inflate storage costs. Deleting them with scheduled scans consumes write capacity. What is the free, built-in solution?
options: DynamoDB TTL — set an expiry timestamp attribute and let DynamoDB delete expired items at no cost
A nightly Lambda that scans and deletes old items
Recreating the table every day
Switching the table to on-demand mode
answer: DynamoDB TTL — set an expiry timestamp attribute and let DynamoDB delete expired items at no cost
explanation: TTL deletes items whose epoch-timestamp attribute has passed, consuming **no write capacity** and costing nothing — built for sessions, tokens, and event data with natural lifetimes (deletions happen within a background window, typically minutes to ~48 h). The scan-and-delete Lambda pays RCUs for the scan and WCUs per delete — the exact cost being eliminated; daily table recreation drops *all* data; capacity mode changes billing math, not data volume.

question: A company's CloudWatch Logs bill keeps climbing. Investigation shows application log groups retain every log line forever. What is the simplest fix?
options: Set retention policies on the log groups so old events expire automatically
Stop logging from the applications
Print logs to stdout without CloudWatch
Create a second account for logs
answer: Set retention policies on the log groups so old events expire automatically
explanation: CloudWatch Logs groups default to **Never Expire** — a quiet cost accumulator. Setting retention (e.g. 30–90 days per compliance needs) expires old events automatically; for logs needed long-term, export to S3 and lifecycle them into Glacier tiers at a fraction of the price. Turning logging off trades cost for blindness; the other options dodge rather than manage the data.

question: Finance wants to be alerted automatically when any service's spending deviates abnormally from its historical pattern — like a misconfigured job tripling NAT gateway costs overnight — without setting fixed thresholds per service. Which tool does this?
options: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
AWS Budgets with one fixed monthly amount
The billing console checked weekly
AWS Trusted Advisor
answer: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
explanation: Cost Anomaly Detection learns each monitored segment's spending pattern with ML and alerts on deviations — no thresholds to define or maintain, with root-cause hints (service, account, usage type). Budgets are excellent for *known* limits but a tripled NAT bill can hide inside a healthy monthly total until too late; weekly manual checks find anomalies after days; Trusted Advisor flags static optimization opportunities, not spend deviations.

question: An organization has 30 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations with consolidated billing. The platform team buys Savings Plans in the management account. A member account starts running matching compute. What happens to the discount?
options: The Savings Plan discount automatically applies to matching usage in ANY account in the organization
Discounts only ever apply in the purchasing account
Each account must buy its own Savings Plans
Discounts apply only if the accounts share a VPC
answer: The Savings Plan discount automatically applies to matching usage in ANY account in the organization
explanation: Under consolidated billing, Savings Plans and RI discounts float across the organization: the commitment first covers the purchasing account's usage, then any member account's matching usage. Volume-tiered pricing (S3, data transfer) also aggregates across accounts. This is why centralizing commitments in one account works — and why discount sharing can be *disabled* per account when chargeback models require it.

question: A company must bring its per-socket Windows Server and SQL Server licenses to AWS. The license terms require visibility and control of the physical sockets and cores the software runs on. Which EC2 option satisfies the licensing terms?
options: Dedicated Hosts — a physical server allocated to you, with socket/core visibility and instance placement affinity
Dedicated Instances — hardware isolation is equivalent for licensing
Standard On-Demand instances with license tags
Spot Instances on isolated hardware
answer: Dedicated Hosts — a physical server allocated to you, with socket/core visibility and instance placement affinity
explanation: BYOL terms tied to physical sockets/cores need Dedicated Hosts: you see the host's sockets and cores, control placement (host affinity), and can use License Manager to track entitlement. The exam's trap is Dedicated *Instances* — also single-tenant hardware, but without socket visibility or placement control, which per-socket licenses require. Tags document licenses; they don't satisfy their terms.

question: A containerized batch-processing service on ECS Fargate tolerates interruptions and reruns failed tasks automatically. Which option cuts its compute cost by up to ~70%?
options: Run the tasks on Fargate Spot capacity
Move the tasks to larger Fargate sizes to finish faster
Switch to ECS on On-Demand EC2 instances
Run the containers on Lambda instead
answer: Run the tasks on Fargate Spot capacity
explanation: Fargate Spot runs tasks on spare capacity at up to ~70% off, with a two-minute interruption warning — the same bargain as EC2 Spot, without managing instances. Interruption-tolerant, retry-capable batch work is its exact profile; capacity providers can mix regular Fargate (for the must-run baseline) with Spot (for the bulk). Bigger tasks bill proportionally more; EC2 reintroduces fleet ops; Lambda has its own limits and pricing model.

question: A storage team managing hundreds of buckets across 25 accounts needs organization-wide visibility into S3 usage: object counts, storage-class distribution, incomplete multipart uploads, and cost-optimization recommendations — in one dashboard. Which tool provides this?
options: Amazon S3 Storage Lens
S3 server access logs parsed manually
CloudWatch billing alarms
S3 Inventory reports per bucket
answer: Amazon S3 Storage Lens
explanation: Storage Lens aggregates S3 metrics across an entire organization into dashboards — storage by class, object counts, incomplete multipart bytes, replication and encryption coverage — with contextual recommendations; advanced metrics add prefix-level depth. Access logs record requests (not inventory), and parsing them across 25 accounts is a project; billing alarms watch totals; per-bucket Inventory reports are the raw material Storage Lens already rolls up.

question: An application writes about 1 TB of log files to S3 daily. Logs are queried frequently for 2 weeks, occasionally for 90 days, and must be deleted after one year. Which TWO lifecycle actions implement this cost-effectively? (Select TWO)
options: Transition objects to a cheaper storage class (e.g. Standard-IA, then a Glacier tier) as access drops off
Expire (delete) objects one year after creation
Replicate the logs to a second Region
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
Convert the logs to Parquet on arrival
answers: Transition objects to a cheaper storage class (e.g. Standard-IA, then a Glacier tier) as access drops off
Expire (delete) objects one year after creation
explanation: Lifecycle rules have exactly these two action types — transitions and expirations — and this access pattern maps cleanly: Standard for the hot 2 weeks, IA at ~14–30 days, a Glacier tier at 90, expire at 365 (which also enforces the retention limit automatically). Replication *doubles* cost; Transfer Acceleration is unrelated; format conversion helps query costs but isn't a lifecycle action.

question: A workload needs 10 EC2 instances running 24/7 as a steady baseline, plus up to 30 extra instances during unpredictable bursts. The burst work is fault-tolerant. Which combination minimizes cost? (Select TWO)
options: Cover the 10-instance baseline with a Savings Plan or Reserved Instances
Serve the burst capacity from Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group
Buy Reserved Instances for all 40 instances
Run all 40 instances On-Demand at all times
Cover the baseline with Spot Instances
answers: Cover the 10-instance baseline with a Savings Plan or Reserved Instances
Serve the burst capacity from Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group
explanation: Layered purchasing matches commitment to certainty: the always-on baseline is predictable → commit for ~60–70% savings; the bursts are unpredictable and fault-tolerant → Spot at up to 90% off, scaled by the ASG only when needed. Reserving all 40 pays for 30 mostly-idle commitments; full On-Demand leaves every discount unclaimed; Spot for the *baseline* risks losing capacity the workload must always have.
